node.label: Eugene Genovese
node.date_label: The Political Economy of Slavery (1965) · Roll, Jordan, Roll (1974) · From Rebellion to Revolution (1979)
node.description: A historian of slavery in the American South whose work joins economic structures, culture and domination. Roll, Jordan, Roll interprets paternalism as a contested relationship of power, not benign treatment. The primary preface and opening retain their own national-culture framing; Walter Johnson’s later review challenges the account’s implications for consent and coercion. A separate reading by N. Gordon Levin discusses the earlier political-economy argument and its problems, preserving the distinction between a named reader’s criticism and Genovese’s own text.
node.representative_figures_and_works: The Political Economy of Slavery (1965; later editions distinct); Roll, Jordan, Roll (1974; preface dated August 1973, Vintage 1976 distinct); From Rebellion to Revolution (1979; 1981 reprint distinct).
node.scope_note: Existing primary preface/opening and named Johnson reading retain all qualifications. Earlier/later political identities do not collapse the writings into one timeless position. Levin is a named substantive reader, not Genovese’s own statement. No direct Gramsci passage has been checked, and acknowledgments do not establish agreement or coauthorship.

incident_edges.relationship: Interprets enslaved culture and paternalism as contested forms within a system of domination.
incident_edges.evidence_note: Existing complete preface and initial paternalism paragraphs, plus Walter Johnson’s complete retrospective, within their recorded scopes. Paternalism is not a benign-slavery claim; Johnson’s consent/coercion criticism remains visible.

incident_edges.relationship: Makes the relation between slaveholding class power, economic organization and development a problem for Marxist historical interpretation.
incident_edges.evidence_note: Specific political-economy intervention mediated by N. Gordon Levin’s substantive review, selected opening pages. This is a contribution to a contested interpretation, not proof that every Marxist shared it, or a direct personal influence from Marx or Gramsci.

incident_edges.relationship: Johnson challenges Genovese’s paternalism/hegemony account and a sharp individual/collective resistance opposition (2001), then specifies objections about revolutionary aspiration, coercive force and resistance in “On Agency” (2003), without saying Genovese ignored enslaved agency.
incident_edges.evidence_note: Two separately dated primary interventions consolidated as one relationship. 2001 scholarly rereading: Johnson challenges Genovese’s paternalism/hegemony account and the sharp opposition between individual resistance and collective revolt, while affirming the book’s lasting value (2001). Complete scholarly rereading. Johnson argues for coerced rule and a continuum of resistance; he explicitly rejects the simplistic charge that Genovese denied enslaved people agency. Original historical examples and Roll, Jordan, Roll remain uncollated. Reading extent: Fresh complete review read through the final day-to-day resistance paragraph. Distinguishes Genovese’s hegemony argument from denying enslaved agency; criticizes paternalism, coerced rule and a strict individual/collective resistance opposition while affirming the book’s value. The original book and historical examples are not independently audited. 2003 “On Agency”: Johnson rejects three premises of Genovese’s resistance/hegemony account while rejecting the claim that Roll, Jordan, Roll simply ignores enslaved agency (2003). The named p. 117 criticism concerns revolutionary aspiration, culture versus coercive force, and the individual/collective distinction. It is not a denial that Genovese discussed resistance. Reading extent: Fresh primary pp113–114,117 and122–123 read; Genovese’s books were not newly read. These are not a single publication or a second independent edge. The original Genovese book and underlying historical examples are not independently collated.

incident_edges.relationship: Genovese adapts Gramscian hegemony to explain how paternalist relations could mediate slaveholding class rule, as Walter Johnson explicates (2001).
incident_edges.evidence_note: Johnson’s own substantive account distinguishes Genovese’s use of hegemony from denying agency and then criticizes its application. Named-reader mediation is explicit; no certification of Genovese’s full book or Gramsci originals. The existing mixed Genovese/Gutman edge_162 stays.

named_group_routes.relationship: informs some historians’ analyses of consent and class relations
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Reception varies among Marxist historians. Genovese is an American example, not a British historian; do not attribute a shared Gramscian method to Thompson and Hobsbawm. Hobsbawm’s1974 review provides a specific British reception: he values Gramsci for studying rebellion while questioning parts of the intellectuals schema. It does not establish Thompson’s agreement or a uniform method.

named_group_routes.relationship: Gramscian resources enter distinct Genovese and Gutman interpretations
named_group_routes.evidence_note: One disputed application within a heterogeneous radical historiography, not the origin of the US New Left. Gutman pp. 584–585 explicitly quotes Gramsci through Tilly on elite perceptions of subordinate groups. Genovese’s hegemony application is supported here by Johnson’s retrospective account; a direct original Gramsci passage in Genovese remains unread. These are different mechanisms and evidence scopes.

named_group_routes.relationship: intersects and contends in interpretations of slavery, resistance, and power
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Black historians’ independent institutions and arguments are not treated as products of the New Left. Genovese’s preface acknowledges alternative national-culture readings; Johnson’s 2001 retrospective review contests consent/coercion in his account. This later assessment qualifies an earlier book without extending mapped coverage.

named_group_routes.relationship: Fox-Genovese defends narrative interpretation and challenges Stone’s assumptions about crisis and progress
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Her December 1978 letter explicitly states that Tuchman does not subscribe to Marxism. This is a supportive critical intervention in reception, not an influence on the completed book or endorsement of every conclusion; Stone’s reply remains visible in the same source.

named_group_routes.evidence_note: His acknowledgments explicitly credit their supplied work and Engerman’s manuscript reading. This resource does not imply acceptance of all their conclusions and does not cancel Gutman’s separate criticism of Time on the Cross.

sources.title: Elizabeth Fox-Genovese and Lawrence Stone, “Tuchman and History,” New York Review of Books, 7 December 1978.
sources.citation: Elizabeth Fox-Genovese and Lawrence Stone, “Tuchman and History,” New York Review of Books, 7 December 1978.

verification.note: Complete letter and Stone reply read. Fox-Genovese challenges professional prestige as a criterion and Stone’s crisis/progress assumptions, defending narrative’s treatment of groups and material dislocation while explicitly distinguishing Tuchman from Marxism. Stone defends differences between synthesis and innovative research and qualifies his progress claim. Tuchman is the subject, not an author of this exchange; neither reviewer’s historical claims are independently verified here.
